metadata.title: Auer v. Robbins, 519 U.S. 452 (1997) (No. 95-897)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: Auer v. Robbins

Opinion filed: 1997-02-19

Docket No.: 95-897

Citations:
• 137 L. Ed. 2d 79
• 117 S. Ct. 905
• 519 U.S. 452
• 1997 U.S. LEXIS 1272

Case holding summaries:
• relying on amicus brief of Secretary of Labor
• "The Secretary's position is in no sense a ` post hoc rationalizatio[n]' advanced by an agency seeking to defend past agency action against attack...."
• relying on litigation documents to determine agency's position
• holding that an agency’s interpretation of its own regulation is “controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation” (internal quotation marks omitted)
• regarding the Secretary of Labor's interpretation of a regulation articulated in an amicus brief
• assessing “the Secretary’s power to resolve ambiguities in his own regulations”
• stating Secretary of Labor’s interpretation was controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation
• holding agency's interpretation of its own regulation to be "controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• defining “consummate” to mean “to bring to comple­ tion”
• in certain circumstances, deference is owed an agency’s reasonable interpretation “of [its] own regulations”
• on the question of whether the Secretary of Labor’s “salary-basis” test for determining an employee’s exempt status reflects a permissible reading of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (“FLSA”
• holding agencies may resolve ambiguities in regulations
• agency's interpretation of its own regulations is "controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulations" (internal quotation marks omitted)
• agency interpretation of its own regulation is controlling unless “plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation.”
• "While the Governor appoints four of the board's five members,. . . the city of St. Louis is responsible for the board's financial liabilities, . . . and the board is not subject to the State's direction or control in any other respect. It is therefore not an `arm of the State'. . . ."
• party cannot challenge agency’s failure to amend its rule in light of changed circumstances without first seeking relief from the agency
• stating that an agency's interpretation of its own regulation is "controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation" (internal quotation marks and citations omitted)
• fact that interpretation comes in form of a legal brief does not make it unworthy of deference
• stating that an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations is controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation
• explaining that courts may defer to an interpretation made in a legal brief so long as it is not a “post hoc rationalization advanced by an agency seeking to defend past agency action against attack” (cleaned up)
• "There is simply no reason to suspect that the interpretation does not reflect the agency's fair and considered judgment on the matter in question."
• holding that agency's interpretation of its own regulations is owed deference
• allowing consideration of an amicus brief containing an agency's interpretation of its own regulations
• holding that courts should generally defer to an agency’s interpretation of its own regulation unless, among other circumstances, that interpretation is “plainly erroneous” (quoting Robertson v. Methow Valley Citizens Council, 490 U.S. 332, 359 (1989)
• holding an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations is “controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation”
• deferring to agency's interpretation of its own regulations as presented in a legal brief
• indicating that the Secretary's interpretations of her own regulations are controlling unless they are plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulations
• holding that an agency’s interpretation of its own regulations is “controlling” unless “plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation” (quotation marks omitted)
• holding that an agency's interpretation of its own regulations is "controlling unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation" (citation and quotation marks excluded)
• deference to agency's interpretation of its own regulation is required unless interpretation is "plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation"
• salary basis test denies exempt status only when employer’s actual practice involves making deductions from pay or a -5- policy creates a significant likelihood of such deductions
• deferring to agency's interpretation of its own regulation
• deferring to agency's interpretation of its own regulation advanced in litigation
• noting that the Commission’s Wireline Competi­ tion Bureau has declined to require an incumbent LEC to bear the entire cost of building new entrance facilities
• explaining that when interpreting a statute and its implementing regulations, we may look to the agency’s interpretation of its own regulations
• determining that a legal brief was a satisfactory vehicle for conveying the agency’s fair and considered judgment
• surveying definitions of “subject to”
• stating that "a `post hoc rationalization' advanced by an agency seeking to defend past agency action against attack" was not entitled to deference but according deference to an agency's amicus brief
• an agency’s interpretation of its own regulation is entitled to deference
• finding that an agency’s reasonable interpretation of its own regulations is entitled to deference
• salary basis test denies exempt status only when employer's actual practice involves making deductions from pay or a policy creates a significant likelihood of such deductions
• deferring to the Secretary of Labor's explicit interpretation of his regulation appearing for the first time in her amicus brief
• agency interpretation of its own regulation must be given controlling weight unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation
• holding that an official's interpretation of his own regulations is controlling unless "plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation."
• agency's interpretation set forth in amicus brief was entitled to deference, where "[t]here is simply no reason to suspect that the interpretation does not reflect the agency's fair and considered judgment on the matter in question"
• an agency’s interpretation of a regulation is not entitled to deference where it is “plainly erroneous” or “inconsistent with the regulation”
• agency's interpretation of its own regulation has controlling weight unless it is plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation
• finding agency’s interpretation of its own regulations is controlling “unless plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation” (quotation omitted)
• suggesting that more than a mere possibility of a deduction is required and holding that an employment manual must "effectively communicate" that pay deductions are an anticipated form of punishment for salaried employees
• An agency's interpretation of its regulation is "controlling unless `plainly erroneous or inconsistent with the regulation.'"
